segments.title: THE STARTER THAT TAKES ITS SOUR
notes: It's Never Too Late To Change
segments.angle: What if this problem existed in an entirely different industry?

sources.text: The Influence Of Others: You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with
It's Never Too Late To Change: No matter how old you are, it's never too late to make a change in your life.
The Influence Of Others: Be with people who see the world in the bigger picture so that THAT becomes your normal frame of mind.
The Choice To Change Is Ours: Either curse the world for being unfair or do all that you can to improve yourself, no matter how little.
The Influence Of Others: Live among your fellow freaks, where obsession is normal and ambition is rewarded.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Last part. Influence and change, in one jar. Go on, then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A sourdough starter, March. It takes its sour from whoever feeds it, and those five people become its whole flavour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bakery now. Fine, we're in a bakery.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And a starter that was sour yesterday can be fed fresh today. It is never too late for the dough.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fresh feed doesn't rise if the jar still sits on the windowsill next to the bins.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then move the jar. Keep it among bakers who bake before dawn, and rising becomes the normal frame of mind.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. Good one. Moving the jar is the easy half.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The hard half is choosing to feed it at all, rather than cursing the windowsill for being unfair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Curse the windowsill, feed the starter. Right, and the bakery isn't fair either.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Live among your fellow freaks, March. Bakers obsessed with rising dough are normal there, and ambition is rewarded.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Obsessed bakers get up in the dark. Nobody mentions that part.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ambition gets rewarded, March. The bread is the reward.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Verdict. You were right that the jar matters. I was right that the feeding does the work.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then we agree on the crust, March. Allow me to sit in your chair and deliver the verdict properly.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sit in that and you'll go flat by lunch.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And Warden of the Graft-Yard? Pick a title that doesn't smell of yeast.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Destiny has a smell, March, and it is yeast. Sit with it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, Your Routine Is Top Priority. Bring flour.

segments.title: THE ROPE THAT FRAYS IN CALM WEATHER
segments.angle: Imagine this idea has been implemented and failed spectacularly one year from now. What are the most likely reasons for its failure? How could we mitigate those risks now?

sources.text: Your Routine Is Top Priority: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel. It doesn't matter how far along you are with something or how much left needs to be done. The moment it's time for the next activity to start, you MUST switch over.
Your Routine Is Top Priority: A schedule makes you act according to the goals of your highest self, not your passing mood.
Your Routine Is Top Priority: If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Your Routine Is Top Priority. Bossy title. It wants us all obeying the timetable like a bus driver with a grudge.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A timetable is a ship's log, March. Every hour is written before the storm, and the crew keeps to it through the worst weather.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Storms don't read logs. Try it on me. One year on, the whole thing has failed spectacularly. I'd switch over mid-sentence every time and hate it by spring.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you are the first casualty, March, and the rest of the crew sails on. A schedule makes you act according to your highest self, not your passing mood.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Highest self, passing mood. Lovely. Tell that to a Tuesday when the mood is the only thing talking. Failure one: it was built for the good days and has no plan for the bad.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the schedule is a mooring, March. A boat holds fast through a gale because the line was fixed before the wind arrived.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A mooring line doesn't snap in a gale. It snaps in calm weather, frayed at one knot nobody bothered to check. That's the failure I'd bet on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Such a simple knot, March. Routine is simple, and simple things endure.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple? Nothing about that knot is simple. Another failure: when it chafes, the note says change the whole schedule, not nudge it. So nobody nudges anything, and the rope rots.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You bristle at the word simple like a cat at a bath, March. Yet you have described my mooring exactly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have stolen my rope, March, and I resent every frayed thread of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stolen? I handed it back. Keep it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then allow me to crown J the Keeper of the Mooring. A title worthy of a man who holds fast.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He can have a title when he's got a loose rope to hold. Keeper of the Line, honestly. Pick a smaller one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Smaller is for shopkeepers, March. Keepers are for ships.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Round one goes to the rule being untested, not wrong. Mitigation: build the bad-day version before the storm, not after.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall keep the knot in my pocket, March, and you may keep your bad-day version. We meet again at the mooring.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next up, the other half of this one. Bring the rope, and don't fray it on the way.

segments.title: THE SWITCH THAT NEVER WAITS
segments.angle: What would this idea look like if I went to its extreme? Could that open up anything interesting?

sources.text: Routine Is Top Priority: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel.
Routine Is Top Priority: The moment it's time for the next activity to start, you MUST switch over.
Routine Is Top Priority: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Routine Is Top Priority: If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Run the extreme. Obey the schedule no matter how I feel. Fine. Feel nothing, switch on the dot.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, March, you propose to sail with the wind tied up in the hold. A bold course, though a pale one, and I doubt the ship would enjoy it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bell rings. I drop the word I was holding. Half a word left in the air.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A bus pulled away from the corner this morning at the exact minute its board promised, and I saw in it the quiet proof that the world keeps its appointments. Some things are meant to be punctual, March, and a half-finished word is simply a word that was never going to be finished.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A bus is a bus. Extreme version: I finish nothing, ever. That's the whole rule.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You make a fine poor example, March, and I am sorry to say that your little experiment is the most persuasive thing I have heard all week. I resent it entirely, and I resent that I resent it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The rule says switch when it's time, not when I'm ready. So my whole day is switches.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then your day is a corridor of doors, March, and every one of them slams before you reach it. Such logic is wonderfully rude, and I wish I had written it, which I have now decided I secretly did.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now the mooring. Tie it tight enough and the boat can't swing with the tide. The rope never frays then. It just snaps.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well, March, the rope returns, and I confess it has grown more interesting in your hands than in mine. A line pulled too taut to yield is a line that cracks all at once, and I should have seen that from the harbour wall.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nothing frays. Nothing bends either. That's the bit nobody checks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The harbour lamp flashes every few seconds and has never once been late, and I call that destiny. The lamp keeps faith with the dark, and the dark never has to ask it twice.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a lamp. It flashes. Nobody's asking its mood.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the lamp has beaten you, March, and you have stopped in the middle of your own argument, which is the one thing your rule forbids. Let it be recorded that I resent being right about you.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hold that thought. I've got one saved. Don't rush me.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall wait the way a harbour waits for weather, March, which is patiently and with a great deal of rope on hand.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next up: the one that asks whether we're enjoying ourselves. Hold the rope loosely.

segments.title: THE BELL THAT NEEDS NO TIDE
segments.angle: What if I had limitless resources or time to solve this?

sources.text: Why Routine Must Be Your Priority: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Why Routine Must Be Your Priority: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Limitless time. Fine. I'd still switch on the bell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, but with unending hours, no bell ever sounds at all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then I hear it late. Still switch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Late is where good intentions go to nap, March, and you have just opened the door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Limitless rope, too. Tie every boat to the wall.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A rope without end, and a harbour without tide. A dreadful kindness, that.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Dreadful? Nothing moves. Nothing frays. Perfect.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Give a man endless hours and he drifts through every one of them. I have watched it happen, and I will not soften it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're describing J. He'd hate that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I describe no one. I describe the harbour wall, which has watched many drifters pass.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harbour wall's smug. Wall's never had a bell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And what did you hide in the rule, March? A trapdoor? A door without a latch?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No trapdoor. Just a bell. Bells don't care about endless.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you hid a bell at the bottom of the boat, and I suspect you knew it all along.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Point mine. Limitless time doesn't fix a bad bell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let the record show the bell is still the only thing ringing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Question, narrator. Who does J spend his time with? Still waiting.

segments.title: THE SLATE THAT STOPS ARGUING
segments.angle: Cross Pollination: Find the intersection of key ideas between two or more notes.

sources.text: Habits Become Automatic - Your New Identity: Build the habit and discipline of following your schedule. If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.
Consistency Compounds Exponentially: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: A schedule makes you act according to the goals of your highest self, not your passing mood.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear it, March. In the old book the keeper wrote the hours on a slate beside the lamp, and once the chalk was set down, the hours kept themselves.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple thing, a slate. Don't call it simple, narrator. That's the whole trick.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simple is what it is, and I say it with love. The slate asks nothing, and the sea does not argue with the slate.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Your highest self picks the hours. Your passing mood gets bored. The slate just stops it arguing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I crown you, then, Lord of the Slate, J. You need never ask the sky what hour it is again.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Lord of the Slate. Lovely. He'd keep the crown in a drawer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A crown in a drawer is still a crown. The legend records it, drawer and all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, the legend keeps your bits. The bit that matters: when the schedule misfires, the note says change the schedule itself, not scribble on it each morning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Overpowered, the book says, and I take the word as it stands. A perfect day that runs itself while the keeper dozes in his chair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Dozes in his chair. Autopilot. That's the overpowered bit, not the chair.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the lamp is lit by habit, and habit has no mood. I find that thrilling, and a little cold.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Cold's fine. Slate's wrong? Rub it out and rewrite it. You don't rub it out late at night because you're tired.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Rubbing out in the dark is the sin the book warns against. Every keeper knows that sin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every keeper knows it. Name one who didn't pick the chalk up late at night.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Name him? Ah. The book is worn exactly there, March, and I am not going to guess.

segments.title: THE CHAIR BOTH OF THEM WANT
segments.angle: How might I solve this in a completely unconventional or exaggerated way?

sources.text: Routine: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel.
Routine: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Routine: If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Closing this one. I'll try the mad version on myself first. I'm the keeper. Chalk's down, lamp's lit, and I'm not allowed out of this chair until the hour says so.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A keeper bound to his chair by his own hand. Magnificent, March, and the book would blush to hear it. The chair itself has been waiting centuries for a worthy occupant.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't say simple. It's a chair and a timer. Say simple once more and I'll ring a bell at you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ring away, then. I shall take the chair while you ring, for a Lord of the Slate must be seated when the hour strikes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's my chair you're eyeing. The lamp's on my side, and so is the kettle.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your chair is a throne in common clothes, and I only wish to see the view from it, which I am sure is splendid.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The view is a wall and a kettle. Verdict, then. I was right. The rule isn't the bell or the slate. It's not rubbing out the hours in the dark. Fix a plan in daylight, and it holds.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You were right, and I am deeply displeased about it, March. You took my simple slate and made a trumpet of it. I had the bones of this story first, the keeper, the lamp and the sea.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bones of it. You had a crown in a drawer. I had a Tuesday and a kettle.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A Tuesday is a small kingdom, and I will rule it, March. Make a note of that, for the legend.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted, and cheap. Your unnamed keeper, the one who never picked up the chalk late. He's the whole point. He just kept his hours in daylight.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A legend need not be named, March. Its silence is its dignity, and its dignity is the lamp.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Legends need names or they're just weather. Fine. The naming goes to J, not you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the book shall have the last word, and I shall hold the pen for it, as the old keepers did.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The book never gets the last word. J does. Up next, Learning - Best Practices, then Novelty - A Life Fully Lived. Keep the chalk dry.

segments.title: THE POSTCARD THAT COSTS NOTHING
segments.angle: How could I design a solution with zero budget?

sources.text: Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Nothing twice. Never eat the same food twice. Never go to the same place twice.
Learning - Best Practices: Just learn one thing, watch the one video, THEN APPLY IT.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Monotony is the enemy. Novelty is the solution.
Learning - Best Practices: You learn the MAJORITY of everything from actually DOING.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Be systematic. Follow guides.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Zero budget, and the note already hands you the plan. Nothing twice. A place you've never been costs your feet and nothing else.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your feet, March? A person who has never once been carried past his own front step will be lifted across the whole world by a single step he has not taken before. Nothing twice is no budget at all. It is an oath, and oaths are priceless.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: An oath that costs nothing is my whole argument. Zero money means you spend attention instead, and you already have that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Attention is a coin the gods mint for very few, and you would spend it on a bus timetable. Mark the sadness of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stop. The note says learn one thing, watch the one video, then apply it. You don't need a grand tour. You need one new street.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the street shall be the first chapter of a great book. On my way to this very sentence I passed a paving stone that rocked beneath my heel like a drumbeat. A sign, surely, March, a summons.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A paving stone that wobbles is a paving stone that wobbles. Whatever sent you past it, it wasn't fate.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have beaten me again, March, and I resent how thoroughly I enjoyed the beating. Let the stone be an ordinary stone. I still say it was waiting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You learn the majority from doing it. So walk the new street, then tell me what it taught you. Otherwise it's a walk with a speech stapled to it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Monotony is the enemy, March, and you would have me file the enemy under habit. Novelty is the solution, and a solution needs no coin, only a willing mind. Monotony costs far more than any ticket.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's a good line. Keep it. Now the plan. Be systematic and follow guides. Free guides are on every phone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Guides! The old map-makers would weep to hear it. Let me chart the route myself, then, in grand ink, upon the finest parchment I can imagine.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ink costs money. A pencil stub and the back of an old envelope cost nothing. Zero budget, remember.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You may have your envelope, March, and I shall keep my ink in the margin where you cannot see it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's the actual idea. The blank postcard stays blank until you go somewhere new. Then it gets one stroke. Zero budget, and a visible record of every first time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A postcard filling with strokes is a fine thing, and I'll concede the monotony you feel on an ordinary Tuesday is the very wall every good day breaks through. The wall is the enemy, and the postcard is its ruin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You were right. Anyway, the first stroke. Who draws it, and where? Pick a street before the afternoon's over.
